lesson.title: When a Certificate Needs to Die Before Its Time
lesson.summary: Certificate revocation lets an authority invalidate an X.509 certificate before its expiration date, using mechanisms like CRLs and OCSP that trade off timeliness, privacy, and reliability.
lesson.body:
Every X.509 certificate carries a validity period, a start date and an end date after which it is no longer considered valid. In an ideal world that expiration would be the only thing anyone needs to check. In practice, certificates sometimes need to be invalidated well before they expire. The private key matching the certificate might be stolen, the certificate authority might discover it issued the certificate to the wrong party by mistake, or the domain it covers might have changed ownership. Waiting months or years for natural expiration in these cases is not acceptable, so certificate revocation exists to kill a certificate's trust early.

The older mechanism is the certificate revocation list, or CRL. A certificate authority periodically publishes a signed list of the serial numbers of every certificate it has revoked, and a verifier is supposed to download this list and check whether the certificate it is examining appears on it. The problem is scale and freshness. A large certificate authority can accumulate an enormous list over time, making it expensive to download and check for every connection, and the list is only ever as fresh as its last publication, meaning a certificate revoked five minutes after the list was published looks perfectly valid to anyone checking against the stale copy.

The Online Certificate Status Protocol, OCSP, was designed to address the freshness problem by letting a verifier ask the certificate authority directly, in real time, whether one specific certificate has been revoked, rather than downloading an entire list. This is faster and fresher, but it introduces its own issues. Querying the certificate authority for every single connection leaks a real time record of exactly which sites a person is visiting to a third party, a genuine privacy concern. It also introduces a reliability dependency: what should a browser do if the OCSP responder cannot be reached at all, because of a network problem or the responder being down. Many browsers historically chose to fail open in that situation, meaning the connection proceeds as if the certificate were valid, since failing closed would break legitimate sites whenever a status check merely timed out. That choice quietly weakens the guarantee revocation was supposed to provide.

A widely adopted improvement is OCSP stapling, where the web server itself periodically fetches a signed, time stamped OCSP response from the certificate authority and attaches it directly to the connection, so the browser never has to contact the certificate authority at all. This solves both the privacy leak and much of the reliability problem, at the cost of the server needing to keep its stapled response current. Revocation, in all its forms, is a reminder that the trust encoded in a certificate is not a fixed fact for its whole validity period, it is a claim that can be withdrawn, and how quickly and reliably that withdrawal reaches every verifier is a real engineering weak point in the whole system.
